text: While deterministic approaches remain quantitative baselines upon which advanced methods improve, they ignore forecast errors and the unpredictable behaviour of consumers with respect to their load demands. These uncertainties introduce volatility in power supply, complicate demand–supply balancing, and challenge both short-term scheduling and long-term investment planning. In networked configurations, such uncertainties can propagate across the system, affecting inter-microgrid coordination and leading to inefficient dispatch, suboptimal exchanges, or even reliability issues. These gaps pave the way for stochastic (SP), robust (RO) and Chance-Constrained (CCP) approaches, especially as they relate to NMGs. For instance, Nikmehr and Rasad’s Monte Carlo reliability analysis confirms that simply interconnecting MGs without any market layer cuts ENS by 70% and system average interruption frequency index (SAIFI) by 55% compared with islanded operation [8]. Seyednouri et al. compressed 200 wind/PV scenarios to 30 and embedded them in a price-setting bilevel MILP; their results showed that each MG operating cost fell by 7.5%, while the DISCO profit increased by 6.9%. Likewise, the loss-of-load risk dropped by 35%, and their sensitivity analysis revealed that supercapacitors below 0.2 p.u. of battery capacity risk jeopardizing all of the positive results obtained [9]. Jani et al. proposed a two stage stochastic optimization approach for the day-ahead and real-time energy management of microgrids; their work reduced the overall system costs by 5.5% and RES curtailment was also reduced by 15% [10]. Karimi et al. developed a multi-objective bilevel model that first maximizes the upper level distribution network operator’s (DNO) profit and then minimizes both the MG independence loss and its energy not served (ENS); their results revealed independence improved by 12% and the ENS dropped 63% without compromising on the profit realized by the DNO [11]. Similarly, Jani and Jadid proposed a two-stage bi-level framework in which a cooperative retail market clears day-ahead energy trades among networked MGs, while a real-time layer re-dispatches every few minutes to absorb renewable and load fluctuations; their results yielded operating cost reductions of $61 and an additional $44 when BESS is included in individual MGs [12]. Where scenario counts explode or tail events are prominent, some researchers have resulted to chance-constrained and robust optimization approaches. Aghdam et al. enforced a 5% violation probability on both emissions and power balance in their networked microgrid formulation. Their results showed that CO2 emissions dropped by 9.2% with a modest 1.3% increase in cost, and tightening epsilon 𝜖 from 10% to 1% increased cost by over 4% [13]. Gao et al. in their work allowed each MG to solve a local robust OPF with polyhedral uncertainty and exchange boundary flows with each other via ADMM; the algorithm converged in a dozen rounds, holding worst-case voltages within ± 3% and at only 1.2% extra cost [14]. To hedge both expected and worst-case costs in networked microgrids, Kim et al. fused a p-robust objective (p = 0.95) with a reduced scenario tree. Results revealed the expected operating cost reduced by 6.4%, while the worst-case cost fell by 12%, revealing a sweet spot between pure stochastic and pure robust formulations [15]. Wang et al. advanced the concept further for combined-cooling–heatingand-power (CCHP) MGs. They formulated a Wasserstein-based two-stage distributionally robust optimisation (WTSDRO) that treated wind power errors as ambiguity sets around the empirical distribution [16]. More recently, Bo et al. demonstrated that robust optimisation can operate at sub-hourly granularity: they embedded a budget-of-uncertainty layer inside a five-minute rolling MILP for an integrated-energy campus microgrid. Column-and-constraint generation solved each window in real time. Their approach reduced worst-case operating cost by about 10% while average cost rose only modestly; crucially, all hydrogen-pressure and thermal constraints remained feasible under every admissible PV/load realizations [17].
